chapters.title: Joshua receives God’s charge

parts.text: After Moses’ death, the LORD commands Joshua to lead Israel across Jordan into the promised land. God assures him of his abiding presence and victory, as he was with Moses. Joshua must be strong and courageous, carefully obeying the law without turning aside. He is to meditate on it day and night and put it into practice, grounding his leadership in God’s command.

Joshua orders preparations for crossing within three days. He reminds Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh that their fighting men must accompany their brethren until all receive rest, though their families remain east of Jordan. They pledge obedience and support, affirm the seriousness of rebellion against his command, and urge him to be strong and courageous.

chapters.title: Rahab shelters the spies

parts.text: Joshua secretly sends two men to inspect Jericho. They lodge at Rahab’s house, and when the king demands them, she hides them under flax and misdirects the searchers. She tells the spies that fear has fallen on the land because of God’s acts at the Red sea and against Sihon and Og. Acknowledging the LORD’s rule in heaven and earth, she asks protection for her family. The spies promise kindness if she keeps their mission secret.

Rahab lowers them from her window in the city wall. They instruct her to tie a scarlet cord there and gather her family inside for safety. After hiding in the hills, they return to Joshua and report that the inhabitants are fainthearted and God has given Israel the land.

chapters.title: The Jordan’s waters stop before the ark

parts.text: Israel moves to the Jordan and prepares to cross. Officers tell the people to follow the ark while keeping the appointed distance, because they have not traveled this way before. Joshua commands them to sanctify themselves, for the LORD will do wonders. God promises to exalt Joshua before Israel and directs the priests carrying the ark to stand in the river.

Joshua announces that the crossing will show that the living God is among them and will drive out the nations. Though Jordan is overflowing its banks, its waters stop when the priests’ feet enter. The upstream water gathers far away, and the flow below is cut off. The priests stand firm on dry ground while the whole nation crosses.

chapters.title: Memorial stones recall the crossing

parts.text: At God’s command, twelve men, one from each tribe, take stones from the place where the priests stand in Jordan. These are to become a memorial, prompting children to ask how God stopped the river before the ark. Joshua also sets twelve stones in the river. The eastern tribes’ armed men cross with their brethren, and the LORD establishes Joshua’s standing before Israel.

After everyone passes over, the priests carrying the ark come out of Jordan, and its waters return to their banks. Israel camps at Gilgal on the tenth day of the first month, and Joshua sets up the twelve stones. He tells the people to explain the crossing to future generations, so all peoples may know the LORD’s mighty hand and Israel may fear him always.

chapters.title: Circumcision, passover, and the LORD’s captain

parts.text: News of Jordan’s crossing leaves the surrounding kings fearful. God commands Joshua to circumcise the Israelite males born during the wilderness years, since the earlier fighting generation had died. The people remain in camp while they recover. God declares that he has rolled away the reproach of Egypt, and the place is called Gilgal.

Israel keeps passover and eats the land’s produce; the manna ceases after they begin eating it. Near Jericho, Joshua meets a man with a drawn sword and asks whether he is for Israel or its enemies. The man identifies himself as captain of the LORD’s host. Joshua falls before him and receives the command to remove his shoe because the ground is holy.

chapters.title: Jericho falls and Rahab is spared

parts.text: Jericho is shut against Israel. God tells Joshua that he has given the city into his hand and prescribes six days of marching around it once daily, with armed men, the ark, and seven priests blowing trumpets. The people are to remain silent until Joshua orders a shout. They follow this pattern as commanded.

On the seventh day they circle Jericho seven times, the trumpets sound, and the people shout. The wall falls, and Israel takes the city. Everything is devoted to destruction except Rahab and those sheltered with her, while precious metals enter the LORD’s treasury. Rahab’s family is rescued because she hid the spies. Joshua pronounces a curse upon rebuilding the city, and his fame spreads as the LORD remains with him.

chapters.title: Achan’s hidden theft brings defeat

parts.text: Achan takes some of Jericho’s accursed spoil, and the LORD’s anger is kindled against Israel. Joshua sends a small force against Ai, but it is defeated, and the people lose courage. Joshua and the elders mourn before the ark. God tells him that Israel has broken the covenant by stealing and concealing what was devoted to destruction. The offense must be exposed and removed before they can stand against their enemies.

The successive selection of tribe, family, household, and man identifies Achan. He confesses taking a garment, silver, and gold and hiding them in his tent. The stolen goods are recovered. Achan, his household, and his possessions are brought to the valley of Achor for judgment, after which the LORD’s fierce anger turns away.

chapters.title: Ai captured and the covenant read

parts.text: God encourages Joshua to attack Ai with the whole fighting force, this time permitting spoil. Joshua places an ambush behind the city while another force approaches openly. When Ai’s defenders pursue the apparently fleeing Israelites, Joshua signals the ambush to enter and burn the undefended city. Seeing its smoke, Joshua and Israel turn on the pursuers and defeat them, capturing Ai’s king.

Ai is destroyed, its spoil taken according to God’s command, and its king executed and buried beneath a heap of stones. Joshua then builds an altar on Mount Ebal as Moses commanded and offers burnt and peace offerings. He writes the law on stones and reads its blessings and curses before the entire assembly, including women, children, and strangers, with the people positioned by Ebal and Gerizim.

chapters.title: The Gibeonites obtain a treaty by deception

parts.text: While other Canaanite kings prepare to fight, the Gibeonites pretend to be travelers from a distant country. Their worn clothing, patched bottles, and moldy bread support the story that they left home long ago after hearing of the LORD’s deeds. Israel examines their provisions but does not seek the LORD’s counsel. Joshua makes peace, and the leaders swear to let them live.

Three days later Israel discovers that the strangers are nearby inhabitants. The congregation complains, but the leaders refuse to break the oath sworn by the LORD. Joshua confronts the Gibeonites, who admit acting from fear for their lives. They are spared but appointed as hewers of wood and drawers of water for the congregation and the LORD’s altar.

chapters.title: God fights for Israel in the southern campaign

parts.text: Five Amorite kings attack Gibeon because it has made peace with Israel. The Gibeonites appeal to Joshua, who marches overnight from Gilgal after receiving God’s assurance. The LORD throws the enemy into confusion and sends great hailstones that kill more than Israel’s swords. Joshua calls for the sun and moon to stand still, and the day is prolonged while Israel defeats its enemies.

The five kings hide in a cave, are captured, and are executed after Israel’s leaders place their feet on their necks as a sign of victory. Joshua then takes a succession of southern cities, including Makkedah, Libnah, Lachish, Eglon, Hebron, and Debir. The chapter attributes the campaign’s success to the LORD fighting for Israel. Joshua and the army return to Gilgal.

chapters.title: The northern coalition is defeated

parts.text: Jabin king of Hazor gathers a large northern alliance with many horses and chariots. God tells Joshua not to fear and commands him to disable the horses and burn the chariots. Joshua attacks suddenly at the waters of Merom and defeats the coalition. He takes Hazor, kills its king, and burns the city, while carrying out the commanded judgment upon the other captured cities.

The account summarizes Joshua’s extended warfare across the land and explains that, apart from Gibeon, the cities made no peace with Israel. God hardened their hearts to meet Israel in battle and receive judgment. Joshua also removes the Anakims from Israel’s hill country, though some remain in Philistine cities. The land is assigned as an inheritance, and it rests from war.

chapters.title: The defeated kings are listed

parts.text: The chapter reviews the kings defeated east of Jordan under Moses. Sihon ruled from Heshbon over Amorite territory, and Og ruled Bashan with its remaining giant population. Their lands were given to Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh. The account describes the main geographical limits of these victories and the eastern inheritance.

A second list records the kings defeated west of Jordan under Joshua, whose lands were assigned to the other tribes. It includes Jericho, Ai, the southern coalition cities, and northern kingdoms such as Hazor and Madon, extending across hills, plains, valleys, and wilderness. Thirty-one western kings are named, providing a consolidated record of the conquests previously narrated.

chapters.title: Land remains to be possessed and eastern shares are recorded

parts.text: Joshua is old, and the LORD points out that much land remains to be possessed, including Philistine and northern coastal territories. God promises to drive out inhabitants but commands Joshua to begin dividing the inheritance among the nine and a half western tribes. The chapter then recalls the lands Moses assigned east of Jordan and notes that some inhabitants were not expelled. Levi receives the LORD’s offerings rather than a tribal territory.

The eastern inheritances of Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh are described by cities and boundaries. The account recalls the defeat of Midianite rulers and the death of Balaam, identified as a soothsayer. It closes by repeating that Moses gave Levi no land inheritance because the LORD God of Israel is their inheritance.

chapters.title: Caleb receives Hebron

parts.text: Eleazar, Joshua, and the tribal family heads begin distributing Canaan by lot, as the LORD commanded Moses. Nine and a half tribes receive land west of Jordan, while the eastern assignments are already settled. Joseph’s descendants form two tribes, Ephraim and Manasseh, and the Levites receive cities and pastureland rather than a separate territorial inheritance.

Caleb reminds Joshua of the faithful report he gave as a spy forty-five years earlier and of Moses’ promise. Now eighty-five and still strong for war, he asks for the mountain country of Hebron, though the Anakims and fortified cities remain there. Joshua blesses him and grants Hebron because he wholly followed the LORD. The chapter closes with the land resting from war.

chapters.title: Judah’s territory and Caleb’s family

parts.text: Judah’s inheritance is described by its southern, eastern, northern, and western boundaries. Within it, Caleb receives Hebron and drives out three sons of Anak. He promises his daughter Achsah to the man who captures Kirjath-sepher; Othniel takes it and marries her. Achsah then asks Caleb for springs of water along with her southern land, and he gives both upper and lower springs.

The chapter lists Judah’s cities by districts: the south, lowlands, hill country, and wilderness, including villages associated with them. These lists define the breadth of the tribe’s inheritance rather than narrating a separate battle for every town. The closing note records an unfinished task: Judah could not drive out Jerusalem’s Jebusites, who continued living alongside them.

chapters.title: Ephraim’s inheritance and the Canaanites at Gezer

parts.text: The inheritance of Joseph’s descendants begins near Jordan and Jericho and extends through the hill country toward the western sea. The account describes the shared outer boundaries associated with Joseph’s lot, which is received by Ephraim and Manasseh. Named towns and landmarks mark the route of the border.

The chapter then describes Ephraim’s particular boundaries and notes that Ephraim also has cities within Manasseh’s territory, each with its villages. The assignment does not mean every inhabitant has been expelled: the Ephraimites fail to drive the Canaanites out of Gezer. Those Canaanites continue living among them and are placed under tribute, leaving foreign inhabitants within the tribe’s inheritance.

chapters.title: Manasseh’s inheritance and Joseph’s request for more land

parts.text: The chapter describes Manasseh’s inheritance, distinguishing Machir’s eastern territory from the western allotments of the remaining families. Zelophehad’s daughters appeal to the command given through Moses and receive shares alongside their male relatives. Boundaries and towns are listed, including cities within neighboring tribal regions. Manasseh fails to drive out some Canaanite inhabitants and later imposes tribute instead.

Joseph’s descendants complain that their allotted land is insufficient for their numerous people. Joshua tells them to clear the wooded hill country. They object that the lowland Canaanites have iron chariots, but Joshua insists that their strength and numbers give them reason to act. They can clear the mountain and drive out the Canaanites despite their power and chariots.

chapters.title: Surveying the remaining land and Benjamin’s lot

parts.text: Israel gathers at Shiloh and sets up the tabernacle. Seven tribes still have not received their inheritances, and Joshua rebukes their delay in possessing the land. Three men from each tribe survey the remaining territory and describe it in seven divisions. They return with a written record, and Joshua casts lots before the LORD at Shiloh to assign the land.

Benjamin’s lot falls between Judah and Joseph’s descendants. Its boundaries are traced from Jordan through the hills and back toward the salt sea. The chapter lists its cities and villages, including Jericho, Beth-el, Gibeon, Ramah, and Jebusi, identified as Jerusalem. These defined borders and settlements establish Benjamin’s inheritance among Israel’s tribes.

chapters.title: The remaining tribal allotments and Joshua’s inheritance

parts.text: The remaining lots assign territory to Simeon, Zebulun, Issachar, and Asher. Simeon receives towns within Judah because Judah’s portion is larger than it needs. The other inheritances are described by boundaries, cities, and villages, locating each tribe among its neighbors. The detailed lists record how the land is distributed by families.

Naphtali and Dan receive their portions next. The account also records Dan’s capture of Leshem and its renaming as Dan. After the tribes receive their inheritances, Israel grants Joshua the city he requests, Timnath-serah in Mount Ephraim, which he builds and inhabits. Eleazar, Joshua, and the family heads finish dividing the land by lot before the LORD at Shiloh’s tabernacle entrance.

chapters.title: The cities of refuge are appointed

parts.text: The LORD tells Joshua to establish the cities of refuge previously commanded through Moses. A person who kills someone unintentionally may flee to one, state the case before its elders, and receive shelter from the avenger of blood. The congregation must judge the matter, and the manslayer remains there until the death of the serving high priest before returning home.

Israel appoints Kedesh, Shechem, and Hebron west of Jordan, and Bezer, Ramoth, and Golan east of it. These cities serve both Israelites and resident strangers. Their purpose is to prevent someone responsible for an accidental death from being killed by the avenger before receiving the hearing required by the law.

chapters.title: Cities for the Levites and God’s fulfilled promise

parts.text: The Levitical family heads remind Eleazar, Joshua, and Israel’s leaders that Moses commanded cities and pastureland for them. Israel supplies these from the tribal inheritances by lot. Aaron’s descendants receive thirteen cities from Judah, Simeon, and Benjamin, including Hebron as a city of refuge, though Caleb retains its fields and villages.

The remaining Kohathites, Gershonites, and Merarites receive their allotted cities from the other tribes, with surrounding pastureland. Altogether the Levites receive forty-eight cities. The chapter concludes that the LORD has given Israel the land he swore to the fathers, granted rest, and delivered their enemies into their hands. None of the good promises he spoke to Israel has failed; all have come to pass.

chapters.title: An eastern altar nearly causes civil war

parts.text: Joshua commends the eastern tribes for helping their brethren and releases them to their homes with a warning to love and obey the LORD. They build a large altar near Jordan. The other tribes fear this is rebellion against God’s appointed worship and prepare for war. Phinehas and tribal leaders confront them, recalling Peor and Achan as warnings that one group’s sin can bring judgment on all.

The eastern tribes explain that the altar is not for sacrifices. It is a witness that they too belong to the LORD, lest future generations deny their share because Jordan separates them. Phinehas and the leaders accept this explanation and report peace to Israel. The altar stands as testimony that the LORD is God.

chapters.title: Joshua’s warning against compromise

parts.text: Now old, Joshua summons Israel’s leaders and reminds them that the LORD has fought for them. Remaining land has been assigned, and God will continue driving out its inhabitants if Israel cleaves to him. They must obey Moses’ law, avoid invoking or serving the remaining nations’ gods, and love the LORD diligently, trusting his strength rather than their own numbers.

If they turn back, intermarry, and attach themselves to those nations, God will no longer drive them out; they will become traps and sources of suffering until Israel perishes from the good land. Joshua reminds the leaders that every good promise has been fulfilled. Just as surely, covenant-breaking and idolatry will bring the threatened judgments upon them.

chapters.title: Israel renews the covenant at Shechem

parts.text: Joshua gathers Israel at Shechem and recounts the LORD’s dealings with their fathers: calling Abraham from beyond the river, giving Isaac and Jacob, delivering Israel from Egypt, preserving them through the wilderness, and granting victories and a land they did not develop. He commands them to put away foreign gods and serve the LORD sincerely. If they refuse, they must choose whom they will serve; Joshua declares his household’s allegiance to the LORD.

The people pledge to serve God, and Joshua warns them of his holiness and the consequences of abandoning him. He records the covenant and erects a stone as witness. Joshua dies at 110 and is buried in his inheritance. Israel serves the LORD through his generation; Joseph’s bones are buried at Shechem, and Eleazar also dies.
